title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators
authors: Xi Wang, Jun Lu, Cheng Zhang, Xiaoying Zhuang, Timon Rabczuk, Hehua Zhu
abstract: Substantial challenges in physics-informed learning have motivated many improvements, but fragmented implementations hinder systematic organization, integration, and comparison. We propose OpenPINN/PINO, an extensible open-source PyTorch framework for physics-informed neural networks and neural operators. Two shared specifications connect problem setup, local computation, and evaluation. Agents support problem formulation, solver planning, and diagnosis. ProblemSpec defines geometry, governing equations, constitutive relations, parameters, initial and boundary conditions, and optional data. MethodSpec configures the model, sampling, loss, optimization, and differentiation. Researchers can register new problem templates and method components, then combine or compare strategies such as Fourier features, residual-adaptive sampling, and self-adaptive loss weighting for a fixed problem. Agents translate natural-language descriptions into specifications, flag missing information, and propose solver plans. The framework validates these specifications and deterministically generates local training and testing code. A diagnostic agent reviews training logs and evaluation results to identify problems and suggest revisions. Three examples show how method choices and agent diagnostics affect accuracy. For viscous Burgers, Fourier features and residual-adaptive sampling each reduced relative $L^2$ error by about $75\%$ from a shared baseline. For periodic Poisson, spectral differentiation reduced mean-free relative $L^2$ error by about $68\%$ across 16 held-out forcings. For a plate with a hole, successive agent diagnoses guided nondimensionalization and optimization. After initial training failure, all three runs met the $10\%$ target, with relative $L^2$ displacement errors of $3.51\%$--$6.31\%$.

infographic.key_insight: OpenPINN/PINO unifies physics-informed neural networks and neural operators through shared specifications, extensible components, and agent-assisted setup and diagnosis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source PyTorch framework supports controlled solver comparisons and reusable workflows for engineering PDE problems.
method: ProblemSpec defines geometry, physics, parameters, constraints, and optional data.
MethodSpec configures models, sampling, losses, optimization, and differentiation for deterministic local code generation.
Agents translate problem descriptions, flag missing information, propose solver plans, and diagnose results.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three examples, selected methods reduced Burgers error by about 75% and periodic Poisson error by about 68% over 16 held-out forcings; agent-guided plate-with-hole revisions achieved 3.51%–6.31% displacement error in three runs.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to three example problems; broader robustness and the reliability of agent-generated specifications require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: OpenPINN/PINO: An Extensible Open-Source Framework for Agent-Assisted Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Neural Operators

title: A Neural Envelope Method for Rapid Gradient-based Optimum Takeoff Trajectory Design
authors: Samuel Sisk, Xiaosong Du
abstract: Urban air mobility arises to mitigate ground traffic congestion. Multidisciplinary analysis and optimization (MDAO) has been introduced to reduce the energy consumption, thereby expanding aircraft performance. Surrogate-based MDAO lowers the cost of optimization, but multimodality disrupts global optimum search for both simulation-based and surrogate-based optimizations. Convex envelopes convert multimodal spaces into unimodal spaces, permitting efficient convex optimization; however, convexifying a design space may produce infeasible "optimal" designs due to complex design constraints. To address these challenges, this work proposes the coupling of a physics-constrained generative adversarial networks (physicsGAN) and neural envelope to transform original, constrained, non-convex optimizations into unconstrained, convex optimizations. Specifically, the physicsGAN discovers a feasible design space where all design candidates inherently satisfy all constraints, by penalizing surrogate-predicted constraint violations during training. Moreover, the neural envelope constructs a neural network-based convex envelope for the transformed objective function within the physicsGAN-discovered feasible space. Note that the neural envelope only needs to deal with objective function since constraints are inherently satisfied in the feasible space. The neural envelope is demonstrated on takeoff trajectory optimizations of the Airbus A3 Vahana eVTOL aircraft. Results show that neural envelopes achieve a 99.91% mean accuracy within a flight-condition space compared with reference convex envelopes. Neural-envelope-enabled optimizations achieve 99.84% accuracy on the global optimum design, costing only 0.04 seconds on average. The neural envelope accelerates the trajectory optimization by 53 and 162 times on average compared to the physicsGAN-enabled gradient-based and global optimizations, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Coupling physicsGAN with a neural convex envelope enables rapid gradient-based search for globally optimal takeoff trajectories within a learned feasible design space.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate energy-efficient eVTOL takeoff planning by reducing the computational cost of constrained, multimodal trajectory optimization.
method: Train physicsGAN to generate feasible designs by penalizing surrogate-predicted constraint violations.
Construct a neural convex envelope of the objective within the learned feasible space.
Use the envelope to replace constrained, non-convex search with unconstrained, convex optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Airbus A3 Vahana takeoff tests, the authors report 99.91% mean envelope accuracy, 99.84% global-optimum design accuracy, and 0.04-second average optimization time—53× and 162× faster than physicsGAN-enabled gradient-based and global optimization, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Feasibility depends on surrogate-predicted constraints, so optimized trajectories need independent physics-based validation, especially outside the evaluated flight conditions.
infographic.paper_title: A Neural Envelope Method for Rapid Gradient-based Optimum Takeoff Trajectory Design

title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?
authors: Shobhita Sundaram, Cansu Sancaktar, Phillip Isola
abstract: LLM agents increasingly drive their own learning. Self-improvement methods delegate various components of model optimization to the models themselves. As models become more capable, this motivates a basic question: do these increasingly capable models still need us to specify how they should self-improve? In this paper we study an autonomous paradigm in which, given basic primitives, resources, and a general goal for self-improvement, agents construct their own self-learning algorithm for context-based optimization. Using the setting of gameplay as a testbed, a frozen LLM agent is given a compute budget and tools for collecting experience and updating text documents, and allowed to freely experiment without an externally imposed loop or access to real-world data. We find that sufficiently capable models do self-improve under these conditions, demonstrating strategies that align with classic cognitive frameworks for self-regulated learning and constructs from machine learning literature on self-generated curricula. Furthermore, we study the extent to which the learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks, observing improvement across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation.

infographic.key_insight: Sufficiently capable frozen LLM agents can devise their own context-based self-improvement strategies without a prescribed learning loop.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent systems may improve through autonomous experimentation and editable text memory without updating model weights.
method: Provide a frozen LLM with a compute budget, basic tools, and a general self-improvement goal.
Let it collect gameplay experience and update text documents without an externally imposed loop or real-world data.
Evaluate whether learned text artifacts transfer to external benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports gameplay self-improvement and transfer gains across different game horizons, mechanics, and 3D navigation, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Success depends on model capability, and the abstract does not establish reliability or compute efficiency beyond the tested settings.
infographic.paper_title: Do LLM Agents Still Need to Be Told How to Self-Improve?

title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI
authors: Giovanni Adorni, Daniele Grosso
abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures. Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence. Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.

infographic.key_insight: Natural Language Programming reframes prompts as cognitive artefacts that coordinate reasoning, goals, constraints, and memory across human–AI workflows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework suggests designing conversational AI systems with explicit goals, validation criteria, and layered memory to support long-horizon reasoning continuity.
method: Extend traditional NLP through distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning.
Introduce Dialogic Working Memory to describe prompts and conversational states as temporary external memory.
Map BTMA, SKGE, and RMR memory architectures onto episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical framework and architecture mapping, but reports no datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: Treating natural language as an executable specification requires validation mechanisms; the abstract does not establish reliable execution or memory coherence.
infographic.paper_title: Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI

title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models
authors: Xiaoyan Hu, Rohit Sonker, Jalal Butt, Jiayu Chen, Egemen Kolemen, Jeff Schneider
abstract: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.

infographic.key_insight: BReaD guides diffusion sampling toward high black-box rewards using a Gaussian process surrogate, without requiring a labeled training dataset or exact reward gradients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets high-dimensional design and discovery problems where objective evaluations are scarce and gradients are unavailable.
method: Fit a differentiable Gaussian process surrogate to queried black-box rewards.
Use Upper Confidence Bound guidance to balance exploration and exploitation during diffusion sampling.
Actively query rewards for generated samples to refine the surrogate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports scientific discovery and image generation experiments showing effective reward optimization in low-data settings, alongside a total-variation-distance analysis.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on surrogate accuracy and uncertainty calibration in high dimensions; the abstract provides no quantitative gains or evaluation budgets.
infographic.paper_title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
authors: Antonio Manjavacas, David Suárez-Caro, Alejandro Campoy-Nieves, Guillermo Rey, Gonzalo Satrústegui, Miguel Molina-Solana
abstract: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

infographic.key_insight: A deep reinforcement learning controller trained in a digital twin maintained prescribed indoor comfort limits after deployment in an occupied home without online fine-tuning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study demonstrates a practical route to coordinating heat pump supply temperature and underfloor heating valves despite slow thermal dynamics.
method: Compare DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations in simulation.
Develop a residential building digital twin and train control agents.
Deploy the best-performing agent in the physical building without online fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulation studies and real-building deployment support comfort maintenance, but the abstract reports no quantitative energy savings or evaluation duration.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to other buildings may require new digital twins and validation of robustness under different operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study

title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
authors: Jiaqi Wu, Yongqi Dong, Yijie Zhong, Maple Shao, Yide Tao, Linsen Cai
abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

infographic.key_insight: Training with bounded trajectory residuals improves a lightweight selector that chooses unmodified candidate trajectories at inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach adapts trajectory selection while keeping the world model and candidate bank fixed, deploying only an 11,725-parameter ranking network.
method: Use PPO to jointly learn candidate selection and bounded residual exploration.
Train context-conditioned candidate preferences from feedback on locally perturbed trajectories.
At inference, combine learned preference and predicted risk ranks with fixed weights; discard the residual branch and critic.
infographic.evidence_signal: On open-loop nuScenes validation, L2 trajectory error decreased 3.99% versus RiskWorld without RL selection and 0.83% versus residual-free categorical PPO under matched feedback and actor-update budgets.
infographic.watch_item: Open-loop trajectory-error gains do not establish closed-loop driving safety or robustness.
infographic.paper_title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model

title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
authors: Aabhash Dhakal, Tim Lachner
abstract: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. Our loss function leverages the true Pareto Frontier, forming a target decision that aligns with a sampled preference vector, and minimizes regret against this target. Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and multi-objective knapsack problems show that our approach outperforms traditional two-stage Mean Squared Error (MSE) baselines. It also surpasses scalarization-based SPO+ approaches.

infographic.key_insight: Pareto-aware decision-focused learning trains predictions to support multi-objective decisions rather than prediction accuracy alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve logistics, routing, and resource allocation plans that must balance conflicting objectives under predicted costs.
method: Extend single-objective SPO+ to multi-objective combinatorial optimization.
Use the true Pareto Frontier and a sampled preference vector to form a target decision.
Train by minimizing regret against that target.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on multi-objective shortest path and knapsack problems report improvements over MSE-trained two-stage models and scalarization-based SPO+, without quantitative results in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Dependence on the true Pareto Frontier may make training computationally challenging for larger problems.
infographic.paper_title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems

title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents
authors: Yicheng Tao, Yuante Li, Zipei Fan
abstract: Agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly forecast real-world events by searching the Web and reasoning over what they find. How well such an agent forecasts depends on both the retrieved evidence and the model, making control over that evidence essential for evaluation. Live evaluations can mix retrieval with reasoning when each system searches on its own, while retrospective search can leak later information through date filters or today's ranking of historical pages. Comparing models, search sources, and memory strategies requires both fixed evidence and a record of how it evolved before resolution. We introduce ForecastGym, which records what four commercial web search APIs return for open prediction-market questions every two days and replays this frozen evidence offline once outcomes are known, comparing models, memory, and captured search sources under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy. Its first release covers 150 questions, 614 evidence states, one per question and collection time, and 131k search results. Rerunning the same queries after settlement returns results that all but state the outcome for up to 92% of the questions, despite the tested date filters. On the frozen evidence, all tested LLMs trail the market in forecasting accuracy. Our diagnostic analysis suggests that missed public information contributes more to the gap in high-gap states than misreading does. Switching the search API changes a model's Brier score by up to 0.043, more than the spread across models, while persistent notes score similarly to rereading all evidence at half the input tokens. The evidence a forecaster sees can matter as much as the model that reads it.

infographic.key_insight: Controlled forecasting evaluations show that retrieved evidence can matter as much as the LLM interpreting it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Freeze and version retrieved evidence to distinguish model reasoning quality from search-source effects and retrospective information leakage.
method: Capture results from four commercial search APIs every two days for open prediction-market questions.
Replay frozen evidence offline after outcomes resolve.
Compare models, search sources, and memory strategies under a fixed evidence-acquisition policy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 150 questions, 614 evidence states, and 131k search results, all tested LLMs trailed the market; switching search APIs changed Brier scores by up to 0.043, exceeding the spread across models.
infographic.watch_item: Retrospective search is not a reliable substitute for archived evidence: post-settlement queries returned outcome-revealing results for up to 92% of questions despite tested date filters.
infographic.paper_title: ForecastGym: A Live, Controlled, and Replayable Benchmark for Forecasting Agents

title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks
authors: Katarzyna Fojcik, Aidas Mikalauskas, Matthias Kampa, Renaldas Zioma, Jogundas Armaitis
abstract: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.

infographic.key_insight: ResoLUT converts trained ResNets into deep lookup-table networks while preserving multi-bit residual streams, achieving strong image-classification accuracy and efficient FPGA inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Layer-wise distillation offers a route from conventional ResNets to hardware-oriented LUT networks without learning logic connectivity from scratch.
method: Distill a trained ResNet layer by layer into LUT trees.
Extract connectivity from the teacher while retaining multi-bit residual streams and BatchNorm.
Use hard LUT decisions during both training and inference to avoid a logic discretization gap.
infographic.evidence_signal: ResoLUT achieves 95.66% on CIFAR-10, 78.87% on CIFAR-100, and 53.69% on 64px ImageNet; a separately optimized FPGA model delivers 90.04% CIFAR-10 accuracy at 189k images/s.
infographic.watch_item: Peak accuracy and FPGA throughput come from different model configurations, so deployment requires evaluating the accuracy–resource trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks

title: Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting
authors: Parmitha Vangapandu, Jonnakuti Pavan Kumar, Sathwik Narkedimilli, MSVPJ Sathvik, T. M. Balakrishnan Nair, Santanu Bhattacharya
abstract: Advection-diffusion priors are a common way to make neural sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts physics-informed. We test where such a prior must enter a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM to help, using daily NOAA OISST v2.1 for the Bay of Bengal (1982-2024) and a synthetic benchmark on the same grid with known currents of controlled strength. (i) On real data, a soft advection-diffusion residual with a learned velocity gives no reliable benefit (lead-15 CRPS -0.007 degrees C, 95% interval [-0.022, +0.008]); a plain temporal-smoothness penalty matches it, and equivalence within 3% is not established either. (ii) Learned velocities do not recover the currents, whether placed in the loss, in an explicit transport step, or in a transport step without neural correction: they correlate with the reference no better than a shuffled-date null, even on synthetic data where knowing the currents would improve day-15 forecasts by 16-23%. (iii) Supplied currents help on synthetic data, but mostly as information: giving them to the network as input channels, without transport, recovers 92% of the transport design's lead-5 gain, and a frozen-current numerical forecast does as well as either. (iv) With GLORYS12 reanalysis currents on real data, the transport design is 6% and 4% worse at leads 1 and 5; reanalysis advection explains essentially none of the daily OISST change (correlation 0.02), and frozen-current transport is worse than persistence. (v) The defect that matters is lead-dependent miscalibration shared by every model. One variance multiplier per lead, fitted on validation data, brings 90% coverage to 0.85-0.91 at all leads and lowers day-1 CRPS by 13-21%; fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts fixes long-lead coverage but costs short-lead skill. This version withdraws an earlier claim of an 81% CRPS reduction that came from an uncontrolled comparison.

infographic.key_insight: For probabilistic SST forecasting, learned advection–diffusion physics offered no reliable benefit, while lead-wise variance calibration consistently improved uncertainty estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Prioritize calibration and verify that current data add predictive information before investing in explicit transport architectures.
method: Compared physics-loss and explicit-transport variants of a heteroscedastic ConvLSTM.
Tested learned versus supplied currents using input channels, transport steps and frozen-current numerical forecasts.
Evaluated lead-wise variance scaling and fine-tuning on 15-day rollouts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests used Bay of Bengal NOAA OISST v2.1 data (1982–2024) and controlled synthetic currents; the real-data physics loss changed day-15 CRPS by −0.007°C (95% interval: −0.022 to +0.008), while calibration reduced day-1 CRPS by 13–21%.
infographic.watch_item: Learned currents were not identifiable in these tests, and reanalysis-driven transport worsened short-lead forecasts; the paper also withdraws an earlier uncontrolled claim of an 81% CRPS reduction.
infographic.paper_title: Where Should Physics Enter? Information, Identifiability and Calibration in Probabilistic Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting

title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis
authors: Minh Luu, Michael Quinn, Aakash Tyagi, David Houngninou, Jiang Hu
abstract: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 reaches every requested quota of compilable bug scenarios that cause at least two test failures, with 14-16 of 16 configured mutation types represented. In completed same-model comparisons, it reduces token use by 6.8x-15.4x relative to BugGen 1.0 and 1.5x-7.9x relative to Firefly. BugGen 2.0 also expands the dataset without simulating every new bug. After finding accepted scenarios with observable failures, it generates alternative mutations at the same locations, simulates only a subset, and estimates acceptance for the rest. This skips 63.6% of AES and 33.9% of FabScalar variant simulations. Full simulation finds that 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants are accepted, with a 1.09% estimation error on the directly comparable FabScalar set. These results show that focusing LLMs on semantic rewriting lowers inference and simulation cost while improving consistency across models and designs.

infographic.key_insight: BugGen 2.0 makes RTL bug synthesis more efficient by assigning structural decisions and validation to deterministic algorithms while reserving LLMs for localized semantic rewriting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower inference and simulation costs can help scale ground-truth RTL bug datasets for debugging tools and testbench evaluation.
method: Use deterministic algorithms for structural analysis, mutation-target selection, and validation.
Use LLMs to generate localized semantic mutations.
Expand accepted bug locations with alternative mutations, simulating a subset to estimate acceptance for the rest.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four OpenTitan IP blocks and FabScalar with three LLMs, BugGen 2.0 met every requested quota of compilable bugs causing at least two test failures; completed same-model comparisons showed 6.8×–15.4× lower token use than BugGen 1.0.
infographic.watch_item: Acceptance estimates do not verify individual unsimulated variants; full simulation accepted 77.7% of AES variants and 95.2% of FabScalar variants.
infographic.paper_title: BugGen 2.0: Rethinking the Roles of LLMs for Scalable RTL Bug Synthesis

title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization
authors: Haihan Zhang, Wendao Wu, Chenheng Zhang, Chunyuan Zheng, Yanyi Li, Cong Fang
abstract: Science advances from frontier to frontier as discoveries reshape what is known and create the basis for further discovery. We present Colombo, a self-organizing AI researcher that drives this renewal, first instantiated in oracle-based optimization. Here, the central question is how efficiently a problem class can be solved through a prescribed information interface and what costs no admissible algorithm can avoid. The gap between achievable guarantees and unavoidable limits defines the frontier recorded in its Complexity Atlas, a living map of frontier settings and the current state of knowledge. Self-Organization turns unresolved gaps into adaptive research programmes, coordinating conjecture formation, mathematical investigation, and replanning as evidence accumulates. Adversarial Co-Ascent develops algorithms and hard families through reciprocal challenge, exposing mechanisms of information use and concealment that guide stronger methods and proofs of unavoidable costs. Independent review and Lean-based formal certification check mathematical claims, while the Long-Term Memory carries supported findings and research experience across settings. To date, Colombo has established optimal or near-optimal rates for more than fifty settings in the Atlas. Colombo thus takes a concrete step toward Autopoietic Science: a scientific process whose validated advances regenerate the conditions of its own progress, continually reshaping how inquiry is organized and what it can discover.

infographic.key_insight: Colombo is a self-organizing AI research system that seeks to close gaps between achievable optimization guarantees and unavoidable computational costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: By pairing algorithm design with lower-bound analysis, Colombo could help engineers understand the best possible performance under prescribed information interfaces.
method: Track known guarantees and unresolved gaps in a living Complexity Atlas.
Adapt research plans while co-developing algorithms and hard problem families through reciprocal challenge.
Check claims through independent review and Lean-based formal certification, retaining findings in long-term memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports optimal or near-optimal rates for more than 50 Atlas settings, but provides no detailed evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify how many reported results received Lean certification or how much human intervention was required.
infographic.paper_title: Colombo: A Frontier-to-Frontier Autoresearch System for Oracle-Based Optimization

title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities
authors: Robin Sharma, Parisa Suchdev
abstract: Web research agents gather information online and write cited reports, including financial analysis. Users can state a priority to guide this research, but a priority may not say how to judge the options, leaving the agent to choose the criteria. We examine how two such agents, built on OpenAI and Anthropic models, interpret a stated priority. In 36 runs, the agents compared Microsoft and Alphabet as businesses. Prompts asked for special attention to growth or resilience, or gave no priority. We analyzed reports, searches, returned sources and cited sources. Of the 24 reports given a priority, 21 focused on it, but their criteria varied. Under the growth priority, OpenAI reports that ranked the companies accounted for risk or predictability and favored Microsoft, while the Anthropic ones judged growth by its pace and favored Alphabet. Under the resilience priority, reports used partly different criteria, and most named Microsoft as the more resilient company. Of the search and source measures tested, only the Anthropic agent's search wording differed detectably by condition. These findings suggest evaluations should examine the criteria behind a report's judgements, not only its focus or accuracy. Interfaces could let users see and adjust those criteria.

infographic.key_insight: Web research agents can follow the same user priority yet apply different judgment criteria, leading to opposing company rankings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Research-agent interfaces and evaluations should expose and test decision criteria, not just topical focus or factual accuracy.
method: Compared OpenAI- and Anthropic-based research agents across 36 runs evaluating Microsoft and Alphabet.
Prompted agents to prioritize growth, prioritize resilience, or use no stated priority.
Analyzed reports, searches, returned sources, and cited sources.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 24 priority-guided reports, 21 focused on the requested priority; growth rankings favored Microsoft in OpenAI reports and Alphabet in Anthropic reports.
infographic.watch_item: Findings cover only two agents and one company comparison, so broader generalization requires additional testing.
infographic.paper_title: How Web Research Agents Interpret User Priorities

title: Projected Penalty-Gradient Tracking for Communication-Efficient Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning
authors: Yanjie Dong
abstract: We investigate communication-efficient federated learning over heterogeneous datasets in the presence of Byzantine adversaries capable of uploading arbitrary information. Penalty-based methods bound the influence of each worker through the bounded gradient of a penalty function; however, the bound is lost once the uploads are compressed, since a Byzantine worker can accumulate an unbounded state at the server. To retain the Byzantine resilience under compressed uploads, we propose a projected penalty-gradient tracking framework, where each honest worker uploads a compressed residual of its penalty gradient and the server projects each reconstructed state onto the known penalty-gradient ball. The framework accommodates any contractive compressor and yields two algorithms: fault-resilient proximal gradient with consistent sparsification (FRPG-CS), whose shared mask is protected by freshly drawn reserve rows, and lazily aggregated FRPG (LAG-FRPG), whose uploads are event-triggered. For smooth and strongly convex losses, we establish a finite-time bound on the expected objective gap, where the Byzantine error floor is independent of the compressor and the compression error decays faster than the optimization error. We also bound the expected number of lazy uploads and derive certificates that separate the finite-penalty model bias from the optimization error. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST show that the proposed algorithms attain the highest accuracy among twelve methods under the Min-Max attack, whereas a compressed-momentum benchmark and a local-update benchmark remain preferable in attack-free accuracy and total traffic, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: Projecting reconstructed penalty-gradient states onto a known ball preserves Byzantine resilience under compressed federated-learning uploads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework reduces communication while preventing malicious clients from accumulating unbounded server-side states through compressed updates.
method: Honest workers upload compressed penalty-gradient residuals; the server projects each reconstructed state.
FRPG-CS uses consistent sparsification with fresh reserve rows; LAG-FRPG triggers uploads only when needed.
For smooth, strongly convex losses, analysis separates compressor-independent Byzantine error from faster-decaying compression error.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST under the Min-Max attack, the proposed algorithms achieved the highest accuracy among twelve methods.
infographic.watch_item: The methods are not universally best: a compressed-momentum benchmark led in attack-free accuracy, and a local-update benchmark used less total traffic.
infographic.paper_title: Projected Penalty-Gradient Tracking for Communication-Efficient Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning

title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models
authors: Aviv Yossef, Or Patashnik, Or Zamir
abstract: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. Semantic watermarks therefore require detection to be robust to content-preserving transformations. Previous methods combining these properties rely heavily on specific white-box properties of the underlying model: either to autoregressive text generation or to diffusion-specific access, such as control of the initial noise or diffusion inversion. In contrast, our construction is fully generic: It only interacts with the generative model and the semantic embedding, a function that determines the notion of "preserving content" under which detection should be robust, via sample and query access. We then instantiate this framework for image generation. We characterize the two competing properties required of the semantic embedding: it should remain stable under transformations that preserve an image's content, but should distinguish independent generations from the same prompt. We train an image encoder directly for this tradeoff. The resulting encoder improves separation while maintaining stability over off-the-shelf alternatives and enables strong aggregate detection while remaining robust to various transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our watermark scheme on both open-source and closed models, which is possible only due to restriction to black-box access.

infographic.key_insight: Semantic watermarking can preserve a generator’s output distribution when averaged over secret detection keys while supporting detection after content-preserving transformations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables watermarking of open-source and closed generative models using only sampling access and semantic-embedding queries, without model internals.
method: Construct a provably distortion-free watermark using black-box generator samples and semantic-embedding queries.
Train an image encoder to balance transformation stability with separation of independent generations from the same prompt.
Use semantic representations for watermark detection robust to content-preserving image changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Image experiments on open-source and closed models report improved encoder separation over off-the-shelf alternatives, maintained stability, and strong aggregate detection under various transformations.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness depends on the embedding’s stability–separation tradeoff; the abstract does not quantify detection performance for individual outputs.
infographic.paper_title: Distortion-Free Semantic Watermarks for Black-Box Generative Models

title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
authors: Nukhbala Gadzhiev, Alexander Morochko
abstract: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.

infographic.key_insight: Lower observation frequency increased prediction error, but frequency-specific RNNs retained a 24–30% advantage over the better kinematic baseline on straight motion and turns at every tested frequency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For sparse V2X observations, a 10 Hz RNN with linear interpolation nearly matched frequency-specific training down to 2 Hz, but was 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz.
method: Downsampled 5 s focal-agent histories from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz to predict 6 s futures.
Compared frequency-specific LSTM RNNs with constant-velocity and constant-acceleration models.
Tested a 10 Hz RNN on linearly interpolated sparse histories, without maps or neighboring agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation used 24,984 Argoverse 2 test scenarios, ten training seeds per main RNN, predefined hypotheses and thresholds, and bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds.
infographic.watch_item: The RNN advantage did not extend to pedestrians, for whom constant velocity was more accurate; results also exclude map and neighboring-agent context.
infographic.paper_title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency

title: Get Hint-Augmented GRPO Done Right Through Activation Steering
authors: Khiem Le, Ting Hua, Nitesh V. Chawla
abstract: GRPO has become the dominant reinforcement learning method for eliciting reasoning capability in LLMs using verifiable rewards. However, it suffers from a fundamental failure mode: when a training question exceeds the base model's current capability, all generated responses fail and receive zero reward, yielding no gradient signal and stalling further capability expansion. An emerging class of GRPO extensions, termed Hint-Augmented GRPO (HA-GRPO), adds a "hint" to the context to reduce the difficulty of the question, thereby producing a usable gradient signal. Nevertheless, existing HA-GRPO methods share a key issue: no hint is available at inference time to append to the question, creating a training-inference context mismatch that leads to inconsistent performance gains. In this work, we reinterpret the function of hinting -- not as reducing question difficulty, but as steering model behavior -- and propose ASH (Activation Steering for Hinting), a novel HA-GRPO method built on this view. During training, the model is presented with both hinted and plain questions, while a trainable steering vector is optimized to widen the margins between the model's generation probabilities for responses to the hinted version relative to the plain version, thereby capturing the question-agnostic component of the behavioral shift induced by the hint. During inference, the trained steering vector is directly injected into the model's activation, reproducing the hint-conditioned behavior without requiring any hint in the context. Experiments with four LLMs (Qwen3-1.7B/4B-Base, Llama-3.2-1B/3B-Instruct) show that ASH consistently improves pass@$k$ on competition-level mathematics benchmarks (AMC, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AIME25) and out-of-distribution benchmarks (Minerva, GPQA-Diamond). Notably, it improves average pass@8 of Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base by \textbf{2.60}\% and \textbf{2.21}\%.

infographic.key_insight: ASH learns an activation steering vector that reproduces hint-induced model behavior at inference without requiring hints in the input.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ASH offers a way to address sparse-reward reasoning training while reducing the training–inference context mismatch of hint-augmented GRPO.
method: Train with both hinted and plain versions of questions.
Optimize a steering vector to widen response-probability margins between hinted and plain inputs, capturing shared hint-induced behavior.
Inject the learned vector into model activations at inference without adding textual hints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models, ASH consistently improves pass@k on competition-math and out-of-distribution benchmarks, with reported average pass@8 gains of 2.60% and 2.21% for Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify activation injection locations or steering overhead, leaving implementation cost and sensitivity unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Get Hint-Augmented GRPO Done Right Through Activation Steering

title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language
authors: Aritra Das, Francesco Cagnetta, Darshil Doshi, Victor V. Albert, Maissam Barkeshli, Andrey Gromov
abstract: Hierarchical models have been proposed as synthetic settings for studying language. However, their relevance to realistic language corpora remains underexplored. In this work, we introduce tree-grams, autoregressive generative $n$-gram models that build the conditional probability tensor $p(x_n \mid x_{1:n-1})$ through a hierarchical composition of order-2 and order-3 tensors. $n$ controls the maximal context window, whereas a rank hyperparameter $d$ controls model capacity, yielding an interpretable and systematically scalable family of approximators of language. We show how tree-grams outperform existing $n$-gram baselines, while remaining competitive with deep transformer-based language models. We demonstrate the utility of such controlled approximations by using tree-grams as generative models. In particular, we show that hyperparameter transfer under $μ$P can be made more robust when narrower models are tuned on simpler data, generated by tree-grams with moderate $n$ and $d$. In addition, we show that entropy and effective range of correlations control performance gap after fine-tuning. This is because tree-grams allow us to explicitly control horizon and capacity. When allowed to route across candidate topologies, we observe emergent sparsity in tree-grams. Such concentrated routing permits pruning upto 95\% of topologies without significant change in performance.

infographic.key_insight: Tree-grams approximate language through hierarchical tensor compositions, with explicit controls for context length and capacity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tree-grams offer controllable synthetic training data that can improve the robustness of μP hyperparameter transfer from narrower models.
method: Construct autoregressive n-gram probabilities using hierarchical compositions of order-2 and order-3 tensors.
Set n to control the maximum context window and tensor rank d to control model capacity.
Learn routing across candidate tree topologies and prune sparsely used routes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports stronger performance than existing n-gram baselines, competitiveness with deep transformers, and pruning of up to 95% of topologies without significant performance change.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify datasets, compute costs, or numerical performance gaps, limiting assessment of practical scalability and transformer competitiveness.
infographic.paper_title: What's in a Tree ? Hierarchical $n$-gram models as controlled approximators of language

title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
authors: Yuanhao Zeng, Shaocheng Lan, Ao Lu, Kuang Yan, Heng Lin, Xinang Xu
abstract: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used. At the candidate level (choosing artifacts), helpful candidate artifacts exist, but selection is no better than random at telling them from harmful ones, so errors accumulate across rounds. At the method level (ranking methods), typical margins of a few percentage points are smaller than the difference between two independent runs of the same method, so published rankings often rest on luck. Together, these findings indicate that agent evolution is often bottlenecked by reliably identifying improvements. This calls for a shift in how we develop and evaluate self-improving agents, from designing ever more candidate improvement systems to making true improvements detectable and accumulable.

infographic.key_insight: Agent evolution can stall because noisy evaluations fail to distinguish genuine improvements from harmful changes, not because better candidates are absent.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Self-improving agent pipelines should prioritize reliable evaluation and selection so real gains can accumulate.
method: Study seven evolution methods across six models.
Assess candidate-level selection of proposed artifacts.
Compare method rankings against independent-run variability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across over 10 million LLM calls, candidate selection was no better than random at separating helpful from harmful artifacts, while typical method margins were smaller than differences between independent runs.
infographic.watch_item: Small reported gains need repeated-run validation before being treated as reliable improvements.
infographic.paper_title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
